title: Dopamine dynamics in a mouse model of temporal lobe seizures with impaired consciousness.
abstract: Focal temporal lobe seizures often lead to impaired consciousness. Recent work has shown depressed cortical arousal, with slow waves and decreased cortical acetylcholine as a possible mechanism for impaired consciousness in focal seizures. However, the role of other key subcortical arousal systems such as dopamine is largely unknown. We aimed to address this gap by investigating dopamine dynamics in a mouse model of focal limbic seizures with impaired behavioral responsiveness. We induced focal limbic seizures by brief electrical hippocampal stimulation in awake head-fixed mice with hippocampal and cortical local field potential recordings. Behavior was assessed by a conditioned auditory response task. We measured cortical dopamine with a genetically encoded fluorescent sensor via fiber photometry. Activity of dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) was recorded by calcium measurements. Focal hippocampal seizures were associated with altered cortical electrophysiological activity and impaired behavioral responsiveness. During seizures, we found sustained increases in dopamine in both medial prefrontal and orbital frontal cortex. We also found increased dopaminergic neuronal activity in the VTA during seizures. Despite these sustained increases, transient task-evoked dopaminergic increases in both cortex and VTA were reduced during seizures. Behavioral responses during seizures were reduced, and auditory stimuli without behavioral responses elicited smaller transient VTA dopaminergic signals compared to stimuli with preserved responses. Together, those results reveal distinct dysregulation of dopamine dynamics across sustained and fast time scales during focal limbic seizures. The sustained increases in dopamine suggest that the altered cortical function and impaired consciousness in focal limbic seizures may more closely resemble encephalopathy or delirium than deep sleep. Depressed transient dopamine release with sensory stimuli could also contribute to impaired behavioral responsiveness during seizures. Further work on the role of dopamine could have important therapeutic implications for altered cognition and behavior in people with epilepsy.

title: Clinical and radiographic outcomes of SpineJack mechanical kyphoplasty versus conservative management in traumatic thoraco-lumbar compression fractures.
journal: The surgeon : journal of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons of Edinburgh and Ireland
abstract: Prospective, comparative, observational cohort study. To compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of SpineJack mechanical kyphoplasty versus conservative management in neurologically intact patients with traumatic thoraco-lumbar compression fractures (AO type A). Thoraco-lumbar compression fractures can be managed conservatively, with prolonged bed rest and rigid orthoses; with minimally invasive techniques originally developed for osteoporotic fractures, such as vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty; or with open or percutaneous pedicle screw fixation. A total of 246 consecutive patients with a Magerl type A thoraco-lumbar fracture were included in this non-randomized prospective study between January 2018 and December 2023. After counseling, 124 patients elected Group A (conservative management: bed rest and a three-point brace) and 122 elected Group B (percutaneous kyphoplasty with SpineJack). At the final 12-month follow-up, 104 patients in Group A and 100 patients in Group B were evaluated, with a total of 42 patients lost to follow-up. The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) were used to assess clinical outcome. Radiographic outcome was assessed by measuring the vertebral height loss rate (HLR) and regional kyphosis angle (RKA). Patients were followed up at 1, 6, and 12 months. Pain relief and recovery of functional ability were significantly better in Group B. Radiographic metrics showed a better outcome in the surgical group. Mechanical kyphoplasty with the SpineJack system is a safe and effective treatment for post-traumatic compression fractures, providing a significant improvement in pain, disability, and radiographic morphometric parameters that is maintained at long-term follow-up.

title: Arthroscopically assisted lower trapezius transfer with semitendinosus autograft in massive rotator cuff tears: a prospective study.
journal: The surgeon : journal of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons of Edinburgh and Ireland
abstract: The optimal management of massive rotator cuff tears associated with absence of external rotation remains unclear. The present study reports the clinical results in patients managed arthroscopically with lower trapezius transfers augmented with free autologous semitendinosus tendon alone or in combination with superior capsular reconstruction with up to 2 years follow-up. Patients treated from May 2019 to July 2024 were enrolled prospectively. Inclusion criteria were pain, inability to elevate and rotate externally the affected shoulder. Preoperative shoulder radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging were collected. Clinical assessment and range of motion evaluation was performed using the VAS, CS, and ASES at 3 and 6 months, at 1- and 2-years follow-up. Shoulder radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging were performed at 6 months and 2 year follow-up. None of the 35 patients originally enrolled was lost at follow-up. In 18 of 35 shoulders, a superior capsular reconstruction using the LHBT was performed. The baseline Constant score was 32 (±16), the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons Shoulder Score was 15 (±9.5) and VAS at baseline was 6 (±2.9). At final follow-up, they improved to 66 (±15.4), 82 (±7.4) and 1 (±1.1), respectively. Range of motion increased from a mean of 90° for forward flexion, from 50° for abduction, and from 0° for external rotation to a mean of 140°, 100° and 48°, respectively. All patients showed statistically significant improvement for all scores and movements, especially external rotation (p < 0.05), at 3 and 6 months. Arthroscopic lower trapezius transfer with autologous semitendinosus augmentation in patients with massive rotator cuff tears with limited or absent external rotation is safe and effective, with predictable pain relief and good clinical outcomes.

title: Altered Brain-cerebrospinal Fluid Dynamics and Juxtacortical Microstructural Alterations in Early-stage Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: Altered cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics may contribute to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but their relationships with cortical microstructure and functional impairment in patients with early-stage ALS (King's stage 1; ALS-ES) remain unclear. Eighty patients with King's Stage 1 ALS and 82 healthy controls underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion MRI, and structural MRI. Global blood oxygen level-dependent-cerebrospinal fluid (gBOLD-CSF) coupling was used as a surrogate measure of brain-CSF dynamics. Juxtacortical free-water fraction (FWF) was quantified across 68 cortical regions. Regional clinical associations were assessed using partial correlations, and indirect effects were estimated using 5000-bootstrap mediation analyses. Spatial correlates of FWF alterations were examined using normative neurotransmitter, cellular, mitochondrial, and transcriptomic maps. After covariate adjustment, gBOLD-CSF coupling was significantly weaker and less negative in ALS-ES than in HCs (pFDR < 0.001). Higher FWF was negatively associated with revised amyotrophic lateral sclerosis functional rating scale scores in the left precentral, left rostral middle frontal, left transverse temporal, and right rostral middle frontal regions after Bonferroni correction. Exploratory mediation analyses identified nominal indirect associations in the left precentral and left rostral middle frontal gyri. Regional FWF abnormalities spatially corresponded to serotonin, gamma-aminobutyric acid, mitochondrial, neuronal, endothelial, and immune-related normative maps. ALS-ES is characterized by altered brain-CSF coupling and spatially patterned juxtacortical extracellular-water abnormalities associated with functional impairment. Normative molecular mapping nominates neurovascular, neuronal, and immune-related contexts for this imaging phenotype.

title: Postoperative delirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing: an exploratory cohort study.
abstract: Advanced age is a major risk factor for both delirium and dementia. A potential early biomarker for dementia is the brain-predicted age difference (brainPAD). We hypothesised that brain ageing accelerates after postoperative delirium (POD), and that increased brainPAD is associated with cognitive decline. Brain MRI scans were obtained in 287 older patients before and 3 months after major elective surgery, and two MRI scans at similar time intervals were obtained in 46 nonsurgical control participants. We computed grey matter brainPAD in patients with POD (POD+), patients without POD (POD-), and nonsurgical controls. The Trail Making Test (TMT) was administered at both time points to examine associations between changes in brainPAD and changes in attention/processing speed (TMT-A) and executive task switching (TMT-B and TMT B-A). Compared with the POD- group, brainPAD increased by an additional 6 (sd=3) months over time in the POD+ group (P=0.002). For each 1 year-over-year increase in brain age gap, patients took 2.3 s longer to complete the TMT-A (P=0.016), whereas no association was observed with TMT-B (P=0.254) or TMT B-A (P=0.91). Postoperativ edelirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing, which in turn is associated with decline in attention and processing speed. These findings help to understand the complex relationship between ageing, delirium, and dementia. NCT02265263.

Intraoperative peripheral perfusion index and mortality after noncardiac surgery: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring primarily targets arterial pressure and flow but might not adequately reflect tissue perfusion. The peripheral perfusion index provides a continuous, noninvasive, and readily available indicator of peripheral perfusion, but its prognostic significance across surgical populations remains uncertain. We hypothesised that greater intraoperative exposure to low perfusion index would be associated with postoperative complications and mortality. In this prespecified multicentre cohort study using electronic health record data, we included adults (≥18 yr) undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac surgery. The primary exposure was cumulative intraoperative area under a perfusion index of 1.5 expressed in PI⋅min. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. The secondary outcome was a 30-day composite of postoperative intensive care unit admission, reoperation, acute kidney injury, or prolonged hospital stay. Among 399 842 patients undergoing 540 101 procedures, a total of 7066 (1.3%) deaths occurred within 30 days: 654 (0.5%) among procedures with no exposure, 1185 (0.6%) in the lower half of exposed procedures, and 5227 (2.6%) in the upper half (split at 3.8 PI⋅min). Compared with no exposure, the adjusted odds ratio for 30-day mortality was 2.18 (95% CI 1.98-2.40, overall association P<0.001) at the 95th percentile of exposure (42.5 PI⋅min), with similar patterns observed across the major surgical specialties. For the composite outcome, the corresponding odds ratio was 1.16 (95% CI 1.14-1.18; P<0.001). Greater intraoperative exposure to low perfusion index was associated with higher postoperative mortality and complications in adult patients undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac surgery. NCT07164339.

title: NRF1 as a sentinel of cellular proteostasis.
abstract: The proteasome bounce-back response is a conserved adaptive program that restores proteasome function when proteasome activity becomes limiting. In metazoans, it is mainly controlled by the cap'n'collar-basic leucine zipper transcription factor nuclear factor erythroid 2-like 1 (NFE2L1/NRF1). NRF1 is constitutively routed through the endoplasmic reticulum and eliminated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system under basal conditions. Proteasome impairment stabilizes ubiquitinated NRF1 and promotes its subsequent maturation in the cytosol, including DNA-damage-inducible 1 homolog 2 (DDI2)-mediated proteolytic cleavage and nuclear translocation. Once activated, NRF1 induces proteasome subunit genes and selected protein quality control pathways to restore proteostasis. This review discusses the molecular organization and regulation of the NRF1-DDI2 pathway, its relevance to cellular homeostasis, and its possible role in cancer, neurodegeneration, autoinflammation, and metabolic stress.

title: Incidence and Factors Associated With Confusional Syndrome (Delirium) in Hospitalized Patients With Severe SARS-CoV-2 Pneumonia in the Intensive Care Unit of a Latin American University Hospital.
abstract: Delirium is a common clinical entity in patients with severe coronavirus disease. We aim to determine the incidence and associated factors for delirium in patients treated in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a Latin American hospital. This retrospective analytical observational study assessed critically ill patients admitted to an ICU during 2020 and 2021. We estimated the incidence of delirium, and multiple risk factors were analyzed, including demographics, hospital courses, lab values, vital signs, surgical exposure, drug exposure, and COVID-19 characteristics. A multivariate logistic regression analysis model was performed to determine independent risk factors associated with the development of delirium. Of 439, the incidence was 28.44%. Initial analysis showed COVID-19 to be more prevalent in those patients who developed delirium. We found that the most prevalent subtype was the mixed motor subtype (43.7%), followed by hyperactive (41.3%), and finally hypoactive (15.1%). The average age was 60.5 years, and most patients were men (66.9%). We found a positive association between ICU inpatients and the use of dexmedetomidine and sedation, while the presence of pronation and higher education are presented as protective factors. Delirium has a higher incidence in critically ill patients admitted to the ICU, with an incidence of delirium at 28.44%. After adjusting for covariates, we found a higher risk of delirium in this cohort and in patients with more extended stays, as well as those where dexmedetomidine was used.

title: Association of the Dementia SomaSignal Test With Metabolic Syndrome-Related Factors in a Community-Based Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: The Dementia SomaSignal Test (dSST) is a plasma proteomics-based predictor of long-term dementia risk, but its clinical correlates in community populations remain unclear. We examined the associations between dSST-based dementia risk and Japanese Specific Health Checkup variables in community-dwelling adults. This cross-sectional study included 220 residents of Arao City, Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan (mean age 64.9 ± 8.5 years; 55.9% women) who underwent both dSST assessment and Specific Health Checkups between March 2023 and December 2024. Associations between the four-level dSST risk category and health examination variables were evaluated using trend analyses and multivariable ordinal logistic regression. Because the continuous dSST risk estimate showed a nonlinear relationship with age, a secondary exploratory analysis of deviation from age-expected risk was performed. Higher dSST risk was associated with older age, male sex, and abnormalities related to metabolic syndrome. In multivariable analysis, greater waist circumference was independently associated with higher dSST risk. In a secondary exploratory analysis using a constructed outcome representing dSST risk above the value expected for age, diabetes was associated with this outcome. These findings characterize the demographic and metabolic correlates of dSST output in a community setting and provide context for its interpretation. Further studies are needed to determine the reproducibility and clinical significance of these associations.

title: Zinc Deficiency Is Associated With Poor Stroke Outcomes Independent of Albumin.
abstract: Zinc is an essential trace element closely associated with albumin and has been implicated in cardiovascular events. However, its association with stroke outcomes, independent of albumin level, remains unclear. We investigated the association between serum zinc level at admission and outcome in patients with acute ischemic stroke. We enrolled 225 consecutive patients with acute ischemic stroke whose admission serum zinc levels were measured. Zinc deficiency was defined as a level < 60 μg/dL and hypoalbuminemia as a serum albumin level ≤ 3.5 g/dL at admission. Associations among zinc deficiency, albumin level, and a poor functional outcome at 3 months (modified Rankin Scale score 4-6) were analyzed. Zinc deficiency was identified in 62 patients (27.6%); these individuals had a lower body mass index and a higher prevalence of chronic heart failure and chronic kidney disease than non-zinc deficient patients. Serum zinc levels were positively correlated with albumin levels (ρ 0.405, p < 0.001). Among 204 patients with available 3-month outcome data, 59 had poor outcomes. Compared with patients with favorable outcomes, those with poor outcomes had significantly higher hypoalbuminemia (55.9% vs. 28.5%, p < 0.001) and zinc deficiency rates (50.9% vs. 16.6%, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis showed that both hypoalbuminemia (odds ratio [OR] 2.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.13-5.34, p = 0.024) and zinc deficiency (OR 2.61, 95% CI 1.17-5.85, p = 0.019) were independently associated with poor outcomes. In acute ischemic stroke patients, zinc deficiency was associated with poor outcomes independent of albumin.

Integrated serum metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics reveal metabolic reprogramming associated with BBB impairment and hippocampal injury in HFD-fed mice.
abstract: Increasing evidence suggests that high-fat diet (HFD) consumption induces systemic metabolic disturbances and is associated with blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and hippocampal injury. This study aimed to explore the potential mechanisms linking HFD-induced metabolic disturbances to BBB and hippocampal abnormalities. Male C57BL/6J mice were fed an HFD or a normal diet (ND) for 12 weeks. Systemic metabolic and inflammatory status, hepatic lipid accumulation, neurobehavioral performance, hippocampal injury, BBB integrity, and hippocampal inflammatory alterations were systematically assessed. Integrated serum untargeted metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics were performed to identify key molecular pathways. HFD-fed mice exhibited systemic metabolic disturbances, increased BBB permeability, hippocampal neuronal injury and inflammation, and impaired motor coordination. Integrated serum metabolomic and hippocampal transcriptomic analyses identified alterations in histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism. Hippocampal transcriptomic analysis revealed upregulation of carnosine dipeptidase 1 (Cndp1) and phospholipase A2 group IVE (Pla2g4e) and downregulation of diacylglycerol kinase kappa (Dgkk) and ethanolamine-phosphate phospho-lyase (Etnppl), which were further validated by RT-qPCR. Serum metabolomic analysis further revealed decreased serum carnosine levels. Given the reported neuroprotective properties of carnosine, we further investigated its effects in palmitic acid-treated HT22 cells. Carnosine improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, and modulated the expression of Cndp1, Pla2g4e, Etnppl, and Dgkk. HFD was associated with BBB impairment, hippocampal inflammatory activation, neuronal injury, and behavioral alterations. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses implicated histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism associated with HFD-induced metabolic disturbances and hippocampal injury.

title: Systemic Treatment Trajectories and Comorbidity Burden in Sarcoidosis: A Retrospective Monocentric Real-World Analysis. Treatment and Comorbidity in Sarcoidosis.
abstract: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease with a variable clinical course. In real-world practice, treatment initiation, tapering strategies, and duration are heterogeneous, and data on the relationship between treatment exposure and comorbidity burden remain limited. We conducted a retrospective monocentric observational study including adults with sarcoidosis followed at a tertiary referral centre from January 2010 to November 2025. Demographic, clinical, radiological, therapeutic, and comorbidity data were extracted from a prospectively maintained database. Associations between treatment variables and documented hypertension and bone mineral density (BMD) impairment were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression. A total of 835 patients were included. At baseline, 81.8% received pharmacological treatment, most commonly corticosteroids alone. Extrapulmonary involvement was present in 45.4% and was associated with treatment initiation and escalation to immunosuppressive therapy. During follow-up, 664 patients received systemic corticosteroids for a mean treatment duration of 38.4 ± 64.3 months, and 25.9% received immunosuppressive agents, predominantly methotrexate. After multivariable adjustment, longer corticosteroid treatment duration was associated with documented hypertension (OR 1.008 per month, 95% CI 1.0002-1.016; p=0.045) and BMD impairment (OR 1.009 per month, 95% CI 1.0002-1.018; p=0.046), whereas initial corticosteroid dose was not significantly associated with either outcome. Longer corticosteroid treatment duration was associated with documented hypertension and BMD impairment. However, unavailable comorbidity onset dates, cumulative corticosteroid dose data, and potential confounding by indication preclude causal interpretation. Prospective studies are needed to clarify treatment-related risks.

title: Targeting long non-coding RNAs to improve therapeutic response in nervous system tumours.
abstract: Despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted treatments, resistance remains a major obstacle in nervous system (NS) tumours. Treatment failure reflects not only individual oncogenic alterations but also adaptive regulatory networks that enable tumour cells to survive therapeutic stress, maintain plasticity and adopt therapy-tolerant phenotypes. Within these networks, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as potential therapeutic targets because of their spatiotemporal expression patterns, context-dependent functions and ability to coordinate gene-expression programmes. Advances in RNA therapeutics provide tools to exploit these properties by targeting disease-associated transcripts and RNA-dependent interactions that are difficult to address with conventional small molecules or antibodies. Studies in NS tumour models have implicated lncRNAs as determinants of therapeutic responses, including DNA repair, apoptotic thresholds, stem-like states, mesenchymal-like plasticity, invasion, metabolic adaptation and stress responses, as well as intercellular communication within the tumour microenvironment. Targeting oncogenic lncRNAs may weaken resistance programmes and enhance the activity of partner treatments, providing a rationale for combinations that could maintain antitumour efficacy at lower drug doses. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for targeting lncRNAs to influence therapeutic response in NS tumours. The evidence is concentrated in gliomas, particularly glioblastoma, with additional studies in other entities. We summarise preclinical evidence for combining lncRNA-directed interventions with chemotherapy or radiotherapy, distinguishing changes in treatment sensitivity and resistance from quantitatively demonstrated synergy. We discuss targeting strategies, including antisense oligonucleotides, siRNAs and interaction-disrupting approaches, and consider translational challenges related to target selection, context-dependent biology, tumour heterogeneity, intracellular accessibility, delivery to tumours and potential toxicity to normal tissues. Collectively, these findings support lncRNAs as potentially actionable regulatory nodes and provide a foundation for developing more effective and better-tolerated combinatorial strategies in NS tumours.

title: Integrating behavioral and molecular biomarkers reveals neurotoxic effects of common insecticide in big brown bats.
abstract: While foraging in croplands, bats are exposed to pesticides that can be neurotoxic even at low concentrations, affecting their physiology and behavior. These sublethal effects are often assessed using molecular biomarkers in isolation, with limited insights into ecological consequences. Here, we used an integrative approach to assess the sublethal effects of chlorpyrifos, a common neurotoxic insecticide, on big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus). We combined behavioral experiments with molecular biomarkers that could reveal the mechanisms underlying observed changes. We orally exposed bats to chlorpyrifos and evaluated their associative memory in a crawling Y-maze, and their stereotyped flight trajectories. To understand the mechanisms behind these behavioral changes, we quantified brain cholinesterase (ChE) activity and used non-targeted proteomics to identify cellular and molecular biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Exposed bats did not change their flight consistency, but were less explorative, had a slower reflex response, and made more incorrect choices in the Y-maze. Exposed bats had a significant reduction in their ChE activity and showed dysregulation of proteins involved in neurological processes like memory, learning, and sound perception. Our results not only provide a comprehensive understanding of the different ways in which pesticides affect individual performance, they also provide a broad description of the underlying cellular and molecular processes, increasing our mechanistic understanding of these effects. Moreover, our results support the sensitivity of behavior as an ecologically relevant biomarker of toxicity and the importance of considering multiple levels of organization to elucidate the mechanisms underlying altered behavior in wildlife due to human activities.

title: Mitochondrial-lipid crosstalk and pharmacological intervention in HPDL deficiency.
abstract: The 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase-like protein (HPDL) converts 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate into 4-hydroxymandelate (4-HMA), an intermediate in an alternative pathway for the generation of 4-hydroxybenzoate (4-HB), a precursor of the Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) headgroup. However, the pathogenic mechanism of HPDL-related encephalopathy and related phenotypes such as spastic paraplegia (SPG83) remains unclear. In this study, we generated an hpdl-/- zebrafish model using the CRISPR/Cas9 methodology. Larvae exhibited microphthalmia, impaired yolk absorption, and a transition from hypokinetic-like to epilepsy-like activity. For the first time in HPDL-related research, we performed extensive lipidomic profiling, revealing a depletion of di- and triglycerides and cholesterol esters alongside mitochondrial membrane instability, marked by decreased acylcarnitines and increased dilysocardiolipins and hydroxy-acylcarnitines, a signature suggestive of impaired β-oxidation and oxidative damage. Bypass and antioxidant therapies using 4-HMA, 4-HB, and the mitochondrial-targeted scavenger MitoTempo were evaluated for their rescue potential. While almost all of the tested drugs successfully rescued the reactive oxygen species production, brain cell death and the altered neuronal activity, we observed that the metabolic recovery occurred independently of the levels of CoQ10 and CoQ9, which remained depleted. Our findings offer support to the hypothesis that Hpdl deficiency causes disease primarily through mitochondrial redox imbalance and lipid metabolic failure, rather than a simple CoQ10 depletion. In spite of unchanged CoQ10 levels, rescue of oxidative stress, brain cell death, and neuronal hyperexcitability in mutant larvae by 4-HMA, 4-HB, and MitoTempo supports a cytoprotective role for these aromatic metabolites, identifies HPDL as a key regulator of mitochondrial homeostasis, and a promising target for aromatic antioxidant therapy.

title: The relationship between regularity of nighttime rest behavior and depressive symptoms in everyday home-life using smartphone-based sensor data.
abstract: Depression is associated with disruptions in circadian and behavioral rhythms. Beyond sleep duration, temporal consistency of sleep-related behavior may represent a relevant aspect of behavioral rhythms. We examine nighttime rest regularity derived from passive smartphone activity data and its association with depressive symptom severity. Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores and self-reported sleep duration were collected via smartphones from 234 individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD; n = 95) or healthy controls (HC; n = 139). Step counts from a 15-day window surrounding BDI assessment were analysed for nighttime intervals (10 pm-8 am), requiring at least seven valid nights. Group differences and associations between nighttime rest regularity, sleep duration, and depressive symptom severity were examined. No significant MDD-HC differences in rest regularity emerged (all p ≥ .058), although estimates descriptively suggested lower nighttime consistency (NCI: β = -0.083) and greater rest-duration variability (LRI-SD: β = 0.118) in MDD. Within MDD, lower regularity corresponded descriptively to higher BDI scores, but no associations survived correction (all p-BH ≥ 0.154). LRI-SD showed the largest positive estimate (β = 0.086, p-BH = 0.154). Self-reported sleep duration was not significantly associated with BDI scores in MDD (β = 0.045, p = .662) or rest regularity variables (|β| ≤ 0.043, all p ≥ .236). Smartphone step count data enable multi-day characterization of nighttime rest regularity. No significant associations with self-reported sleep duration emerged, suggesting distinct behavioral characteristics. Associations with depressive symptom severity showed small descriptive tendencies but remained nonsignificant after correction, warranting investigation.

title: The Association between Physical Activity and Higher Corticolimbic Synaptic Density is Independent of Body Mass Index.
journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
abstract: Regular physical exercise has been linked to biomarkers of slowed biological aging, including brain aging, though the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. Exercise may enhance neuroplasticity and attenuate synaptic decline; however, evidence supporting these effects has largely been limited to animal and postmortem studies. Whether physical activity is associated with synaptic density in the living human brain remains unknown. We used positron emission tomography (PET) with the radiotracer [18F]SynVesT-1 to quantify synaptic density in vivo in 51 individuals (61% female). Participants were classified as physically active or insufficiently active, and group differences in synaptic density across corticolimbic regions were examined. Additional regression and mediation analyses assessed associations among physical activity, synaptic density, body mass index (BMI), and depressive symptom severity. Physically active individuals exhibited significantly higher synaptic density across corticolimbic regions compared to insufficiently active individuals (F6,44=2.41, p=0.042). These effects remained marginally significant after adjusting for BMI and depressive symptom severity (F6,42=2.33, p=0.050). Region-specific regression analyses further demonstrated positive associations between physical activity and synaptic density. Mediation analyses indicated that BMI did not account for the observed relationships. These findings provide the first known in vivo evidence that physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density in the living human brain, particularly within prefrontal circuits. Results suggest that exercise may support synaptic integrity through mechanisms partially independent of BMI. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine causality, characterize temporal dynamics, and evaluate whether physical activity may serve as a scalable intervention to preserve synaptic health.

title: Flow-induced endothelial lipid dysregulation in ischemic stroke: from mechanotransduction to therapeutic implications.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) induces significant and sustained alterations in cerebral hemodynamics, which extend beyond the acute phase and actively contribute to post-stroke cerebrovascular remodeling. Accumulating evidence suggests that endothelial cholesterol and neutral-lipid homeostasis is a critical determinant of vascular integrity, whereas its dysregulation may promote endothelial inflammation, and vascular remodeling. Abnormal shear stress, particularly low and oscillatory shear stress, may connect post-stroke hemodynamic changes to endothelial lipid dysregulation by regulating lipid uptake, intracellular lipid processing, cholesterol efflux, and lipid storage through mechanotransduction pathways. Although direct evidence demonstrating that altered shear stress drives endothelial lipid accumulation in the cerebral vasculature remains limited, findings from endothelial studies and mechanobiology suggest a functional "flow-lipid axis" implicated in post-stroke vascular pathology. In this review, we summarize the hemodynamic alterations following IS and how abnormal shear stress may regulate endothelial cholesterol and neutral-lipid homeostasis through mechanosensors and downstream pathways, including AMPK, mTOR, SREBP, and lipophagy. We further identify the existing gap in causal evidence connecting post-stroke hemodynamics to cerebral endothelial lipid accumulation, and propose targeted translational research avenues aimed at facilitating the development of hemodynamic- and metabolism-based therapeutic strategies for IS.

title: Correlates of Consultant Disposition Recommendations in the California Child and Adolescent Mental Health Access Program.
abstract: The California Mental Health Access Program (Cal-MAP), a statewide child psychiatry access program, offers remote telephonic psychiatric consultation to pediatric primary care providers (PPCPs) statewide. This study investigated patient, provider, and practice-level factors associated with Cal-MAP disposition recommendations following telephonic psychiatric consultation. This cross-sectional study included unique patient consultations conducted from March 2022-June 2023 (N=1,295). Descriptive statistics and logistic regression assessed differences in post-consult recommendations (i.e., remain in PPCP care for mental and behavioral health [MBH] needs or referral to specialty care) based on the PPCP's consultation question, patient clinical and sociodemographic characteristics, psychiatric complexity, current MBH supports, PPCP type, and practice setting. Most consults involved Non-Hispanic White youth (N = 494, 47.6%), females (N = 652, 50.4%), adolescents aged 12-17 (N = 724, 55.9%), and those without psychiatric complexity (N = 769, 59.4%). Continued PPCP care was recommended for most consults (N = 959, 74%). Compared with consultations without psychiatric complexity, those with complexity (one indicator: adjusted OR [aOR], 0.32; 95% CI, 0.23-0.44; ≥2 complexity indicators: aOR, 0.18; 95% CI, 0.12-0.27) had lower odds of recommendations for continued PPCP management. Consultations involving households with a primary language other than English had lower odds than those involving English-speaking households (aOR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.35-0.93). Telephonic psychiatric consultation through Cal-MAP supports MBH management by PPCPs, with the majority of consults recommended for continued primary care management. Consults involving psychiatric complexity and household languages other than English were associated with specialty referral recommendations.

title: SLC15A3 contributes to diabetic encephalopathy through enhancing mitochondrial lipoperoxidation-mediated microglial activation.
abstract: Diabetic encephalopathy (DE) is a common central nervous system complication of diabetes, characterized by cognitive decline and neuroinflammation. Mitochondrial dysfunction is closely implicated in DE pathogenesis, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, by intersecting published diabetes-associated microglial genes with mitophagy-related genes, we identified SLC15A3, which was highly expressed in microglia. SLC15A3 overexpression induced microglial activation, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, manifested by increased IBA-1 expression, enhanced migration, elevated ROS and MDA levels, and upregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Conversely, SLC15A3 knockdown effectively reversed high glucose (HG)-induced microglial oxidative stress and inflammatory activation. Mechanistically, Nucleotide-binding Oligomerization Domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2) was identified as a candidate interacting protein of SLC15A3. SLC15A3 upregulated NOD2 expression to activate the downstream JNK/DRP1 signaling axis, thereby aggravating mitochondrial lipid peroxidation, reducing mitochondrial membrane potential, and triggering aberrant PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy dysregulation. Notably, JNK knockdown significantly rescued SLC15A3-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. Importantly, this SLC15A3-NOD2 regulatory axis was further validated in primary murine microglia. In a microglia-endothelial co-culture blood-brain barrier (BBB) model, SLC15A3 silencing alleviated HG-evoked BBB permeability damage and restored the expression of tight junction proteins. In vivo hippocampal knockdown of SLC15A3 or NOD2 mitigated BBB disruption, reduced neuronal apoptosis, and partially attenuated cognitive deficits in DE mice. Collectively, this study demonstrates that SLC15A3 facilitated mitochondrial lipid peroxidation and mitophagy dysregulation via a NOD2-dependent JNK/DRP1 pathway, thereby accelerating BBB injury and DE progression. SLC15A3 represents a potential therapeutic target for diabetic cognitive complications.

title: Isolation, identification and prebiotic potential of polysaccharides from fresh goji berry.
abstract: Polysaccharides from fresh goji berry were isolated and characterized to investigate their structures, simulated gastrointestinal digestion, and lactic acid bacteria (LAB) growth-supporting effects. Hot-water extraction, 50% ethanol precipitation, and chromatographic separation yielded two acidic polysaccharides, LBP1 and LBP2, with apparent molecular weights of 13.47 ± 0.24 and 185.0 ± 3.0 kDa, respectively. Methylation analysis and NMR spectroscopy suggested that LBP1 possessed a highly branched pectic structure, whereas LBP2 had a predominantly homogalacturonan-like backbone containing methyl-esterified galacturonic acid residues. Arabinose-containing side chains and minor rhamnose residues were also identified. During simulated digestion, LBP2 was relatively stable in the salivary phase, whereas gastric and intestinal digestion were accompanied by a shift toward lower molecular weights, an increasing trend in reducing sugars, and changes in monosaccharide composition. Preliminary LAB growth-support assays were performed in supplemented MRS medium using Lactiplantibacillus plantarum GH-6, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus KK-21, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum GH-8. After 48 h cultivation at the additive concentrations of 3, 4, and 1 mg/mL for LBP2, viable counts of GH-6, KK-21 and GH-8 were 9.11 ± 0.06, 9.16 ± 0.11, and 8.86 ± 0.05 log(CFU/mL), respectively. Compared with the blank controls, LBP2 significantly increased the viable counts of GH-6 and KK-21 (P 0.05). These findings indicate strain-dependent LAB growth-supporting effects of LBP2 under the tested conditions.

title: Dual Guidance in Regional Anesthesia: Influence of Needle Electrode Configuration on Stimulation Success at the Sciatic Nerve: A Randomized, Controlled Pilot Trial.
Anticoagulants compared with aspirin in patients with embolic strokes of undetermined source: an individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised trials.
abstract: Direct-acting oral anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent stroke compared with aspirin in randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS), and subgroup benefits suggested by analyses of individual RCTs were inconsistent across trials. We aimed to evaluate the effect of anticoagulation on the risks of recurrent stroke and major bleeding in patients with ESUS, overall and in prespecified subgroups using individual participant data from RCTs. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE and Scopus for RCTs published between April 1, 2014, and March 1, 2025, without language restriction, comparing anticoagulants with aspirin in patients with ESUS. Non-randomised studies and studies not enrolling patients with ESUS were excluded. We requested individual participant data from the principal investigators of all eligible trials. The primary outcomes were recurrent stroke and major bleeding. For each outcome of interest, we estimated the treatment effect for the overall trial population separately within each trial and the resulting overall treatment estimates were subsequently pooled across trials. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (version 2.0) for the primary efficacy outcome of stroke recurrence. Hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% CIs were estimated following adjustment for prespecified covariates and pooled by use of the random-effects model. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025644724). Our systematic database search identified 1170 records. Of these studies, four were eligible for inclusion in the analysis, including a total of 13 970 participants. Mean age of participants was 66 years (SD 10·6); 5486 (39·3%) participants were female and 8484 (60·7%) were male. Across all trials, 6989 patients were assigned to receive a direct-acting oral anticoagulant and 6981 were assigned to receive aspirin. The hazard for recurrent stroke was similar between participants allocated to anticoagulant or aspirin (399 of 6989 patients [4·6 events per 100 patient-years] in the anticoagulant group vs 417 of 6981 [4·8 events per 100 patient-years] in the aspirin group; adjusted HR 0·94, 95% CI 0·78-1·14), without evidence of heterogeneity across studies (I2=5%, p for Cochran's Q test=0·37). The hazard for major bleeding was also similar between the two groups (149 of 6989 patients [1·6 events per 100 patient-years] in the anticoagulant group vs 106 of 6981 [1·1 events per 100 patient-years] in the aspirin group; adjusted HR 1·19, 95% CI 0·52-2·73), but heterogeneity was present across studies (I2=79%, p for Cochran's Q test=0·0023). Anticoagulation did not reduce the risk of recurrent stroke after ESUS when compared with aspirin, and the risk of major bleeding did not differ significantly between the two treatments. A possible benefit from anticoagulation in patients with ESUS and left atrial enlargement, as shown in a hypothesis-generating subgroup analysis, should be investigated in future trials. title: BDNF-TrkB signaling is involved in the histopathological damage, synaptic protein loss and inflammatory response caused by an electromagnetic pulse in rat brain cortex: Erratum.
Galectin-3 could aggravate blood-brain barrier disruption after intracerebral hemorrhage through inhibiting toll-like receptor 4 ubiquitination degradation in cerebral vascular endothelial cells.
abstract: The key mechanism underlying secondary brain injury (SBI) after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) involves compromised blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, primarily characterized by injury to brain endothelial cells (BECs). Galectin-3 (Gal-3) could exacerbate SBI post-ICH through its active involvement in neuroinflammation. Gal-3 thus represents a promising target for SBI. This study aimed to elucidate its role in BBB dysfunction. In vivo, a C57BL/6 ICH model was established by collagenase injection. In vitro, the human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMECs) were cultured with hemin to mimic the BBB microenvironment and treated with exogenous Gal-3 or conditioned medium. After ICH, Gal-3 inhibited the ubiquitination and degradation of toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) mediated by Triad3A through specific binding to TLR4 on the surface of BECs, resulting in abnormal accumulation of TLR4 protein. This directly activated the TLR4/MyD88/nuclear factor kappa B signaling pathway, thereby upregulating the expression of MMP-9, causing degradation of substrate membrane proteins and tight junction proteins, which then caused increased BBB damage. This study confirmed that Gal-3 could specifically bind to TLR4 protein in BECs and inhibit its ubiquitination degradation, resulting in abnormal accumulation of TLR4, which then activated matrix metalloproteinases-9-mediated tight junction proteins and basal membrane proteins degradation, ultimately breaking the integrity of the BBB. This study would contribute new knowledge regarding the pathological mechanisms underlying BBB impairment in ICH, thereby facilitating the development of more effective approaches for preventing and treating SBI.

title: DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features.
abstract: Molecular analyses of brain regions implicated in risk are essential to providing insights into the antecedents and consequences of psychiatric disorder. In the current study, we contrast the genome-wide DNA methylation levels in the postmortem brains of individuals with a primary diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD; N = 101), major depressive disorder (MDD; N = 101), and controls (N = 100). We demonstrate: (1) the potential role of adult trauma in PTSD-associated oligodendrocyte reductions in the amygdala, (2) an association of MDD with differential methylation within the amygdala that may be accounted for by cell type enrichment, (3) sex- and diagnosis-specific multi-omics factors within the methylome that differentiate the immune and other biological pathways involved in PTSD, and (4) illustrate the lack of concordance in DNA methylation across brain regions in PTSD compared to MDD. We also find a brain-based biological aging factor that may provide insights into the biological pathways of brain aging.

title: Targeting toxic gain-of-function mutations in Alexander disease.

title: Spectral envelopes of facial movements predict intention, cortical representations, and neural prosthetic control.
abstract: Animals use coordinated facial movements to sample the environment, ingest nutrients, and communicate. Rodents produce rhythmic facial movements during spontaneous behavior and cognitive tasks. Measuring these movements precisely and linking them to neural activity remains challenging. We introduce face-rhythm, an unsupervised pipeline that combines markerless point-tracking, spectral analysis, and non-negative tensor decomposition to reduce facial video to a small set of interpretable components. Applied to videos of mice performing Pavlovian conditioning, a brain-machine interface task, and free behavior, face-rhythm recovers whisking, sniffing, licking, and subtler motifs. The resulting components are consistent across animals, decode task variables and internal states, and explain cortical activity with a low-rank representation. Facial motor cortex neurons are predicted well by a phase-invariant spectral transformation of movements above roughly 0.5 Hz, whereas slower movements retain a phase-variant representation. Face-rhythm compares favorably with deep-learning tracking and embedding methods while yielding an interpretable description of facial behavior.

title: Human cardiac organoids innervated by autonomic neurons using a mixoid approach model myocardial infarction under hypoxia.
abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived organoids are powerful models of human development, disease, and drug discovery, but most lack innervation, limiting physiological relevance. We developed a simple, versatile method to generate innervated cardiac organoids, termed mixoids, by mixing neural and cardiomyocyte progenitors. Using human sympathetic and parasympathetic cardiac mixoids (hSCMs/hPCMs), we investigated autonomic regulation of human heart development. Sympathetic innervation was associated with functional coupling, improved cardiac architecture, enhanced transcriptional metabolic maturation, and shifted cellular composition toward an atrial cardiomyocyte (ACM) identity. Under hypoxia, hSCMs recapitulated myocardial infarction features including adrenergic overload, calcium mishandling, fibrosis, and apoptosis, which were reduced by the beta-blocker propranolol. Parasympathetic innervation similarly transcriptionally enhanced metabolic maturation and shifted the cardiomyocyte composition toward maturity and promoted an atrial-conduction system-associated identity. These findings establish cardiac mixoids as a platform to study autonomic regulation of heart development and disease and a potential strategy for generating other innervated organoids.

title: Occupational differences in sickness absence among older health and social care workers: A population-based longitudinal cohort study.
abstract: As retirement ages increase and working lives are extended, work capacity and potential differences between occupational groups become increasingly important. This is particularly relevant in the health and social care sector, which employs a large share of older workers. Occupational differences in sickness absence have been observed among younger health and social care workers. However, it is not known whether such differences exist among older health and social care workers. Examine whether there were occupational differences in sickness absence among older female and male health and social care workers. Longitudinal cohort study using nationwide register-based microdata. The health and social care sector in Sweden. All 63,998 women and 14,920 men who turned 65 in 2015-2018, lived in Sweden throughout ages 60-65, and worked in health or social care organisations for at least one year at ages 60-64. Occupation at age 64 (exposure) was classified into Managers, Physicians, Nurses, Psychologists/Social workers, Assistant nurses/Care assistants, Other health professionals (e.g., physiotherapists), Teachers/Educators, Administration/Customer service, Highly qualified non-medical occupations (e.g., lawyers), and Facility/Maintenance workers (e.g., cleaners). Sickness absence (outcome) was examined separately at ages 60-64 and 66-69. Hurdle models were used to estimate the association between occupation and the odds of any sickness absence (>14 days), as well as sickness absence length, measured as the number of net days among those with sickness absence, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Analyses were stratified by sex and work status at ages 66-69 (in paid work/not in paid work) and adjusted for sociodemographic and work-related covariates. Each occupation was compared with the weighted mean sickness absence rate and length across all occupations. Occupational differences were observed in the odds of sickness absence among both women and men, regardless of work status at ages 66-69. Assistant nurses/care assistants had consistently higher odds of sickness absence (CI range women: 1.10-1.25; men: 1.08-1.37), while managers (CI range women: 0.42-0.70; men: 0.35-0.88) and highly qualified non-medical occupations (CI range women: 0.43-0.73; men: 0.43-0.84) had lower odds. Occupational differences in sickness absence length were mainly observed among individuals who did not work at ages 66-69. Sickness absence and remaining in paid work after age 65 are not equally distributed across occupations among older health and social care workers. These differences should be considered when developing policies and workplace measures to support extended working lives. The study was preregistered with OSF (reg. no. 4snxp).

title: Bergmann glia: The silent architect shaping cerebellar cortex.
abstract: The cerebellum is a brain structure that regulates motor functions and cognitive processes. Recent molecular and embryological studies have clarified its cellular development and the intercellular interactions that guide it. These studies have provided a framework for exploring molecular mechanisms underlying pattern formation, neurogenesis, fate determination, and prenatal and postnatal cell migration. This article focuses on the development, structure, identifying markers, and function of Bergmann glial cells (BGCs), which are crucial for the folding of the cerebellar surface, the proper functioning of the cerebellar neuronal circuit, and nervous pathology. BGCs offer a promising therapeutic target for central nervous system (CNS) disorders, with impaired cells being linked to abnormalities seen in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), long-term synaptic depression (LTD), and vanishing white matter (VWM). In conclusion, the evidence positions BGCs as active organizers of cerebellar circuitry and as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets whose disease-specific roles require further mechanistic validation.

title: Something's gotta give: Reward-induced effort modulation in task-switching reveals a flexibility-stability trade-off.
abstract: Everyday behavior requires balancing two control modes: flexibility, for switching between tasks, and stability, for maintaining goals in the face of interference. One influential account posits that these modes trade off, such that increased flexibility comes at the cost of reduced stability. However, empirical support for this trade-off remains equivocal. We propose that it arises from reward-induced effortful control modulations during tasks that require both modes simultaneously. Across two experiments (N = 80 and N = 87), participants completed a task-switching paradigm in which cued reward incentives were manipulated over varying timescales. Large rewards increased flexibility, evinced by reduced task switch costs, but reduced stability, evinced by increased incongruence costs. In Experiment 1, this trade-off also emerged across blocks, with fluctuations in stability and flexibility inversely related under reward. Overall, these findings provide evidence for a reward-driven flexibility-stability trade-off, in which higher incentives promote flexibility at the cost of stability.

title: Emotion recognition training across sensory modalities: Comparing the effects of multisensory and unisensory training.
abstract: Emotion-recognition training is widely used to improve emotion recognition and, by extension, social competence, yet few studies compare unisensory and multisensory training. We randomly assigned adults to auditory, visual, audiovisual, or control training using a validated protocol adapted across modalities, and assessed emotion recognition with auditory, visual, and audiovisual tests. The primary analysis used first-response accuracy, analysed by ANCOVA with pre-test as a covariate; a similarity-based scoring method and a normalized-gain index served as robustness checks. All trained groups improved reliably from pre- to post-test across modalities, but the untrained control group also improved, indicating that part of this within-group change reflects task exposure. On the primary measure, no trained group reliably exceeded control, audiovisual training did not outperform unisensory training, and no trained-modality advantage emerged. In secondary comparisons using the more sensitive similarity-based metric, the trained groups exceeded control on overall recognition, and the audiovisual and auditory groups also exceeded control on their trained modality. Improvement in the trained groups extended to untrained modalities. Audiovisual stimuli were also recognized more accurately than unisensory stimuli at baseline and in the control group at post-test, a perceptual rather than training effect. Consistent with a preregistered prediction, basic emotions were recognized more accurately than social emotions, with no reliable differences by training condition. Overall, brief training improved emotion recognition on the similarity-based measure, and improvement extended to untrained modalities. We found no evidence that any single training modality, including audiovisual, was superior. Its value likely lies in matching the nature of everyday emotion.

title: Maternal TPOAb positivity is associated with offspring neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.
abstract: Maternal thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb) positivity increases offspring neurodevelopmental risk, but the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We combined mouse experiments and human cohort analyses to investigate the effects of maternal TPOAb exposure. Mice offspring were assessed for maternal antibody transmission, placental pathology, blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, neuroinflammation, and neurotrophic/synaptic signaling pathways. Human data were used to examine the mediating role of placental inflammatory factors in the association between maternal TPOAb positivity and offspring cognitive function. Through mouse experiments, we observed that in utero TPOAb exposure resulted in sustained high maternal antibody levels and was associated with transplacental passage. This exposure was associated with significant placental pathology, including reduced placental volume, diminished vascularity, and upregulated expression of inflammatory cytokines. TPOAb was detectable in the fetal circulation and brain parenchyma. Offspring exhibited BBB disruption (reduced claudin-5, occludin, and ZO-1 protein expression) and persistent hippocampal neuroinflammation accompanied by morphological evidence of microglial activation and altered bulk hippocampal expression of the myeloid-associated markers CD16 and CD206. Despite unaltered neuronal density, sustained alterations in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) and synaptic signaling pathways (PSD-95, synapsin-1, CREB) were observed. In an exploratory mediation analysis of the human cohort, placental inflammatory factors statistically accounted for 9.9-25.7% of the association between maternal TPOAb positivity and offspring cognitive function, consistent with partial mediation. These findings suggest a placenta-dependent pathway whereby maternal TPOAb positivity is associated with placental inflammation and antibody transfer, followed by fetal BBB compromise, persistent microglial activation, and altered neurotrophic and synaptic signaling, collectively contributing to offspring neurodevelopmental risk.

title: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) as outcome in clinical trials in multiple sclerosis: current use and evidence-based sample size considerations.
abstract: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is a biomarker of disability progression and progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) in multiple sclerosis (MS). Planning trials with GFAP as an outcome requires plausible effect sizes and variability from empirical evidence. To assess how GFAP is used as an outcome in MS studies and to derive evidence-based scenarios for sample size calculations. We searched PubMed, Embase and trial registries, pooled estimates in meta-analyses, and used these alongside Swiss MS Cohort variability estimates to inform five scenarios. As of February 2026, 28 clinical studies used GFAP as an outcome, half unpublished; most were small and rarely used GFAP as a primary outcome. Two trials showed significant reductions, both small (EXPAND 8%; SUNBEAM 11%). Pooled treatment effect was small (between-group difference in mean log-change -0.03; 95% CI -0.08 to 0.02). A 1:1 randomized trial would need 352 patients to detect a 14% GFAP reduction, fewer than 52 for 33%, and at least 1100 for 5%. GFAP remains an exploratory outcome; measurement, analysis and reporting are heterogeneous, treatment effect estimates are small and uncertain. Most current studies are underpowered; this work provides empirical guidance for designing conclusive trials with feasible sample sizes.

title: TSPO-SPECT imaging as a possible biomarker of disease progression in patients with Multiple Sclerosis: A Danish pilot study.
abstract: Reliable biomarkers for disease progression in multiple sclerosis (MS) are lacking. Translocator protein (TSPO) expression is increased in microglia and other cell types during neuroinflammation, and TSPO imaging is widely used as an in vivo marker of neuroinflammatory processes. While TSPO positron emission tomography (PET) shows promise, its clinical use is limited by cost and logistical challenges associated with the use of short-lived radiotracers. To evaluate TSPO single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) using 123I-CLINDE as a potential biomarker for disease monitoring and prediction of disability progression in MS. Nine patients with relapsing-remitting MS and high disease activity underwent TSPO-SPECT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at baseline and 6 months after initiation of ocrelizumab. TSPO polymorphism rs6971 was assessed. Tracer uptake was quantified as total distribution volume (VT) in normal appearing white matter (NAWM). Disability was measured using the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) at baseline and during 2-year follow-up. Associations between early change in NAWM VT and later change in EDSS were analyzed using Spearman's correlation coefficient. Changes in NAWM VT were heterogeneous across participants. NAWM VT increased in 3 patients, was unchanged in 2, and decreased in 4. A significant association was observed between change in NAWM VT and change in EDSS (Spearman's rho = 0.844, 95% confidence interval 0.25 to 1.00, p = 0.004). Patients with increased NAWM VT showed greater disability worsening, while those with decreased NAWM VT generally improved. No relapses were reported during follow-up. TSPO-SPECT with 123I-CLINDE shows potential as a biomarker for chronic compartmentalized CNS inflammation and may reflect chronic disease progression. However, the results of our study are limited by a small sample size, and larger controlled studies are needed to validate its clinical utility.

title: Novel insights into BPS-induced neurodevelopmental toxicity in the octopus: Excitation/inhibition imbalance associated with GRM5 dysregulation potentially impairs learning and memory function of Amphioctopus fangsiao.
abstract: Bisphenol S (BPS) is widely detected in aquatic environments, yet its neurodevelopmental toxicity mechanisms in marine invertebrates remain poorly understood. Octopuses, the most intelligent invertebrates with sophisticated nervous systems, serve as ideal model organisms for neurodevelopmental research. In this study, Amphioctopus fangsiao embryos were exposed to 1, 10, and 100 μg/L BPS to evaluate its neurodevelopmental toxicity. The results showed that BPS exposure reduced hatching rates, and induced structural atrophy in the vertical lobe, a core region responsible for learning and memory, accompanied by oxidative stress, neuronal apoptosis, and synaptic damage in brain tissue. Behavioral assays confirmed that 10 μg/L BPS was associated with altered light habituation behavior, suggesting a potential impact on non-associative learning. Through transcriptomic analysis and molecular docking, we prioritized glutamate receptor 5 (GRM5) as a candidate neurotoxic target. BPS was predicted to interact with GRM5 and to upregulate its expression, which was associated with disruption of neuronal excitatory/inhibitory balance, inhibited the ERK/CREB pathway phosphorylation and downregulated synaptic plasticity-related genes. These findings propose a putative mechanistic framework linking GRM5 dysregulation to potential learning and memory impairment, providing an integrated assessment of BPS-induced developmental neurotoxicity in a cephalopod with complex cognition and a basis for future risk assessment.

title: A four-year longitudinal study on the acute and chronic DBS neuromodulation effects in Parkinson's disease.
Pain in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder: Findings from longitudinal and deep-phenotyping cohorts.
abstract: Pain is a common non-motor symptom in Parkinson's disease, yet whether it emerges in the prodromal period and whether it reflects underlying dopaminergic degeneration remains poorly characterized. Our objectives are threefold: to determine whether pain is elevated in polysomnogram-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), whether it predicts phenoconversion to overt synucleinopathy, and whether it is associated with regional dopaminergic deficits. Participants with iRBD (n = 507) and demographically-matched controls (n = 33) enrolled in the North American Prodromal Synucleinopathy (NAPS) Consortium from August 2018 through July 31, 2025 were analyzed. Pain was assessed using MDS-UPDRS item 1.9. Cox proportional hazards models - including a time-varying model incorporating repeated assessments - examined pain as a predictor of phenoconversion. Dopamine transporter (DAT) SPECT imaging was performed in a subset (n = 244), and ordinal logistic regression models evaluated associations between regional striatal binding ratios and pain severity. An independently recruited clinically enriched chronic pain cohort (n = 110) with and without RBD underwent detailed pain phenotyping without neuroimaging. Participants with iRBD had significantly higher odds of greater pain severity than controls (OR = 2.24, 95%CI 1.17-4.49, p = 0.02). Moderate-severe baseline pain predicted phenoconversion (HR = 2.21, 95%CI 1.13-4.32, p = 0.02), an estimate that remained stable after adjustment for several medical covariates, although the overall three-category model was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). Cross-sectional striatal DAT binding was not associated with symptom severity. Despite greater subjective pain burden, objective pressure algometry did not differ between iRBD and controls. Pain may represent a prodromal symptom of synuclein-based neurodegeneration but was not associated with striatal DAT binding, suggesting that nigrostriatal terminal loss alone does not explain the association.

title: Naphthalimide-based fluorescent probe for visual detection of nitric oxide in living cells and zebrafish.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy
abstract: Aberrant nitric oxide (NO) levels are closely linked to inflammation, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disorders and cancers. It is therefore urgent to develop reliable approaches for real-time, in-situ detection of NO in living organisms. Herein, a new NO fluorescent probe T1 was rationally designed and synthesized using naphthalimide as the fluorophore based on the specific cyclization reaction between o-phenylenediamine and NO to form benzotriazole. It displayed a remarkable fluorescence turn-on response with around 10-fold fluorescence enhancement toward NO, showing favorable concentration, time-dependent sensing and selectivity. The probe could sensitively detect exogenous NO and endogenous NO stimulated by lipopolysaccharide in macrophages. Moreover, it successfully visualized elevated NO in LPS-induced inflammatory cell models, rotenone-triggered Parkinson's disease (PD) cell models and zebrafish in vivo, demonstrating favorable tissue permeability and in vivo applicability.

title: Validation and reliability of the Epilepsy Self-Stigma Scale (ESSS) in Italian.
abstract: Self-stigma is the interiorization and acceptance of prejudicial beliefs of one person's culture of origin. Higher levels of self-stigma in epilepsy negatively affect quality of life and outcome. We investigated self-stigma in people with epilepsy (PwE) in Italy, by translating, culturally adapting and validating the Italian version of the Epilepsy Self-Stigma Scale (ESSS). For psychometric validation, the scale (together with GAD7, NDDI-E, QOLIE31 and RSES) was filled-in by 87 adult PwE anonymously and voluntarily participating to an online survey broadcasted on "Fondazione Epilessia LICE ETS" social media. Clinical and demographic data were collected. Internal consistency was good (Cronbach's α = 0.74). Reliability was high (Omega Total = 0.87). Higher stigma scores were moderately associated with greater anxiety (GAD-7; ρ = 0.43, p < 0.001) and depressive symptoms (NDDI-E; ρ = 0.39, p < 0.001). Negative correlations were observed with self-esteem (RSES; r = -0.45, p < 0.001) and quality of life (QOLIE-31; ρ = -0.42, p < 0.001). Individuals with lower levels of independence showed higher stigma scores. The 8-item Italian version of ESSS is valid and reliable. The findings suggest self-stigma is closely associated with quality of life through psychological factors, particularly self-esteem, although relationships should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design.

title: Tuning in: Multi-tissue networks regulating intestinal stem cell biology.
abstract: Organ plasticity depends on the collective ability of cells to adapt reversibly to internal and environmental changes. In adult tissues, stem cells drive this adaptability in cooperation with a dynamic microenvironment, known as the stem cell niche. In vivo studies have revealed the multiorgan and multidimensional nature of adult stem cell niches. The intestinal epithelium exemplifies remarkable tissue plasticity, supporting both homeostatic self-renewal and rapid injury repair. This review summarises emerging multi-tissue signalling networks that regulate adult intestinal stem cell function. We focus on intestinal stem cell interactions with vascular and neuronal microenvironments, as well as broader inter-organ communication that supports intestinal regeneration. We also examine how these pro-regenerative mechanisms may be exploited in disease.

title: Chromone- and coumarin-triazole hybrids as multitarget-directed ligands for neurodegenerative diseases: Neuroinflammation and oxidative stress modulation.
abstract: Neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders arise from the interplay of multiple pathogenic mechanisms, including dysregulated arachidonic acid metabolism, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. In this framework, the development of multifunctional small molecules capable of simultaneously modulating interconnected biological pathways represents an attractive therapeutic strategy. In this paper, we report the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of a series of chromone- and coumarin-triazole derivatives as multitarget ligands combining anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. The compounds were firstly tested for COX-1/COX-2 and mPGES-1 inhibition, and the most promising ones were evaluated for their antioxidant properties, modulation of the Keap1-Nrf2 protein-protein interaction, immunomodulatory and neuroprotective activities in microglial cells, and plasma stability. Finally, the compounds endowed with the most balanced multitarget activity were assayed in the whole-organism Caenorhabditis elegans model. Preliminary structure-activity relationship studies demonstrated that the chromone scaffold was consistently superior to the corresponding coumarin counterpart, and compound 1a emerged as the most potent dual COX-2/mPGES-1 inhibitor, displaying nanomolar COX-2 inhibition together with submicromolar mPGES-1 and Keap1-Nrf2 inhibitory activities, measurable antioxidant properties, and satisfactory plasma stability. Compounds 3a and 5, more stable than 1a, exhibited a less potent but more balanced multitarget profile. In particular, 3a effectively promoted a shift of activated microglia toward a reparative phenotype, whereas 5 showed significant neuroprotective activity in C. elegans, protecting against 6-OHDA-induced dopaminergic neurodegeneration and improving locomotor function in an α-synuclein transgenic model. Overall, this work identifies chromone-triazole core as a versatile platform for the development of multifunctional ligands simultaneously targeting inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways. The complementary biological profiles of compounds 1a, 3a, and 5 provide promising starting points for the optimization of novel therapeutic agents against neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Fluvoxamine exerts neurorestorative effects via the Sigma-1 receptor in two mouse models of dopaminergic degeneration.
journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
abstract: The selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor fluvoxamine has high binding affinity for the Sigma-1 receptor, an intracellular chaperone protein modulating neuroplasticity and pro-survival pathways. We set out to examine the effects of fluvoxamine in mouse models of dopaminergic degeneration driven by neurotoxin-induced damage or seeded alpha-synuclein aggregation. In mice with unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine lesions, five weeks of daily treatment with fluvoxamine at the doses of 0.3 or 20 mg/kg/day gradually restored contralateral forelimb use and partially protected nigral dopaminergic neurons while reducing the number of phagocytically activated microglia. In addition, the larger dose significantly increased the density of dopaminergic fibers in the dopamine-depleted striatum. These beneficial effects were absent in Sigma-1 receptor knockout mice. We next evaluated the 20 mg/kg dose in mice inoculated with preformed alpha-synuclein fibrils in the striatum, starting treatment one month post-surgery and administering it daily for four months. Although fluvoxamine did not alter the formation of alpha-synuclein inclusions, it promoted a regenerative response in the nigrostriatal pathway, increasing dopaminergic fiber density in the depleted striatum and markedly reducing the number of activated microglia in the substantia nigra. The results from both parkinsonian models demonstrate that fluvoxamine treatment stimulates fiber regrowth in the damaged nigrostriatal system while inhibiting microglial overactivation. These findings support Sigma-1 receptors as a potential target for disease-modifying therapies in Parkinson's disease and point to fluvoxamine as a relevant repurposing candidate.

title: The niacin receptor HCAR2 alleviates depression-like behaviors by suppressing microglial NLRP3 inflammasome and complement-mediated synaptic pruning.
journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability, yet current antidepressants are limited by treatment resistance and delayed onset. Neuroimmune inflammation and aberrant synaptic pruning are core pathological drivers, but targeted therapeutics remain scarce. Hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 (HCAR2), a microglia-enriched GPCR and the target of niacin, has shown anti-inflammatory potential, but its role in depression is unknown. Using a chronic unpredictable mild stress mouse model with bidirectional HCAR2 manipulation, we found that chronic stress impaired hippocampal HCAR2 signaling. Niacin robustly alleviated depressive-like behaviors, whereas HCAR2 knockout markedly attenuated these effects and exacerbated stress vulnerability. Mechanistically, HCAR2 activation suppressed hippocampal neuroinflammation and microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation via a non-canonical, ARRB2-dependent endocytic pathway: activated HCAR2 internalized into microglial endosomes, bound NEK7, and blocked NLRP3 inflammasome assembly. Concurrently, HCAR2 preserved synaptic integrity by inhibiting complement C3/CR3 signaling and attenuating excessive microglial synaptic phagocytosis. In conclusion, HCAR2 acts as an endogenous protective regulator in depression via dual mechanisms: ARRB2-mediated endosomal sequestration of NEK7 to suppress NLRP3 inflammasome, and inhibition of complement-driven synaptic pruning. These findings identify HCAR2 as a promising therapeutic target and provide a rationale for repurposing niacin in MDD treatment.

title: Neutrophil-hitchhiking and microglia-homing liposomes co-delivering artemisinin and edaravone for cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury treatment.
abstract: Clinical outcomes of cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) remain unsatisfactory, largely because the blood-brain barrier (BBB) restricts the delivery of most neuroprotective agents to the brain parenchyma. Although artemisinin (ART) and edaravone (EDV) have shown promising therapeutic potential for CIRI, their clinical application is hindered by their short in vivo half-lives and poor aqueous solubility. Neutrophil infiltration triggered by CIRI provides a unique opportunity for drug delivery across the BBB, whereas targeted modulation of microglia represents a key strategy for mitigating reperfusion-induced injury. However, existing neutrophil hitchhiking delivery systems primarily focus on BBB traversal and generally lack a secondary targeting mechanism to promote preferential drug accumulation within the inflammatory core of the ischemic brain. Here, we developed a dual-modified liposomal system functionalized with sialic acid (SA) and phosphatidylserine (PS) (ART/EDV-PS/SAL) for the co-delivery of ART and EDV. This system enables sequential two-step targeting through SA-mediated neutrophil hitchhiking for BBB traversal, followed by PS-mediated microglial homing within ischemic brain tissue. In a mouse model of CIRI, ART/EDV-PS/SAL markedly reduced cerebral infarct volume, preserved BBB integrity, and significantly improved neurological and behavioral outcomes. Mechanistically, ART/EDV-PS/SAL exerted neuroprotective effects by suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation, attenuating pyroptosis, and promoting microglial polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. By harnessing endogenous immune cells to achieve efficient and sequential drug targeting, this study establishes a promising nanodelivery platform for the treatment of ischemic stroke and other neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Visual-field position shapes input sampling and output routing in the superior colliculus.
abstract: The location of visual stimuli influences the actions animals select, reflecting the distinct ecological and behavioral significance of the upper and lower visual fields. In mice, the superior colliculus transforms visual information into defensive and approach behaviors, with its superficial layers containing genetically defined cell types with distinct projections. Whether these circuits are repeated across visual space or are specialized by visual-field position remains unclear. Dual-color rabies tracing demonstrated that wide- and narrow-field neurons receive input from a largely shared set of brain regions, whereas upper- and lower-field domains sample these inputs differently. Some regions preferentially innervate one visual field domain; others contain spatially segregated neurons innervating each domain.
